legal.headline: Movie is not IT software even if delivered via digital link or hard disk: Bombay High Court
legal.hook: Movie is not IT software even if delivered via digital link or hard disk: Bombay High Court
legal.summary: The Bombay High Court has ruled that cinematograph films do not qualify as 'IT software' under Indian tax law, even when delivered via digital link or physical hard disk. The judgment clarifies the boundary between two distinct categories of goods under the Customs Tariff Act and GST regime. The court rejected arguments that the medium of delivery—digital or physical—transforms a movie into software. This distinction matters because IT software enjoys specific tariff classifications and GST treatment that differ from films. The ruling emerged from a case involving the classification of digitally-delivered or disk-based motion pictures for customs and excise purposes. No word yet on whether the losing party will appeal to the Supreme Court, but the decision settles a recurring classification dispute that has affected distributors and streaming platforms operating in India.
legal.contextNote: This implicates Section 98 of the Customs Tariff Act (HS Code classification) and the GST classification rules under the IGST Act. Films fall under the 'motion pictures' category, while 'computer software' has its own tariff entry—a distinction the court anchored in the *essential nature* of the content, not its wrapper. For in-house counsel at streaming platforms (Netflix, Amazon Prime, SonyLiv, etc.) and theatrical distributors: (1) audit GST and customs filings for 2020–present to ensure films were not erroneously classified as 'software' at lower rates; (2) confirm that digital delivery contracts with content partners reflect correct tariff classification to avoid demand notices from customs authorities; (3) if any pending assessments exist, this judgment provides strong legal cover to contest reclassification as software and claim refunds. No direct Supreme Court precedent on this point exists; this fills that gap.

legal.headline: Forcing parties into mediation is always a bad idea: Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani
legal.hook: Forcing parties into mediation is always a bad idea: Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani
legal.summary: Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani of the Bombay High Court has stated that forcing parties into mediation is inherently problematic. The remark appears to have been made in the context of court-ordered or mandatory mediation schemes, where judicial direction compels unwilling disputants to participate in alternative dispute resolution (ADR) processes. The Justice's position signals judicial skepticism toward blanket mediation mandates, suggesting that meaningful settlement requires genuine consent and willingness from both sides. The statement reflects ongoing tension within Indian courts between promoting ADR (a policy priority since the Alternative Dispute Resolution Division thrust under the National Action Plan for Implementation of the Nyaya Bandhu Scheme) and respecting party autonomy. The remark carries particular weight given Justice Bhambhani's seniority and the Bombay High Court's influence over commercial dispute handling in India's largest financial hub.
legal.contextNote: This touches Section 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (court-annexed mediation) and the Supreme Court's repeated push under the Mediation and Conciliation Rules, 2016 and subsequent guidelines. *S. Sundaresan v. Union of India (2013)* and *National Legal Services Authority directives* have favoured facilitative ADR, but Justice Bhambhani's remark flags a counter-position: mandatory participation may violate consent-based principles fundamental to settlement efficacy. For in-house counsel: (1) when served with court-ordered mediation notices, document client's reluctance and strategic objections on record—forced participation may later undermine settlement validity or waiver arguments; (2) if negotiating ADR clauses in fresh commercial contracts (particularly with Reliance or fintech counterparties), explicitly carve out mandatory pre-litigation mediation to preserve litigation strategy; (3) watch for Bombay High Court judgments citing this remark when challenging mediation orders on grounds of party autonomy or waiver of prejudice.

legal.headline: CCPA: Rapido’s pre-ride tipping prompts misleading and unfair; ₹10 lakh penalty imposed
legal.hook: Holding that Rapido’s pre-ride tipping prompts misled consumers into believing that additional payments would improve ride availability and confirmation, the CCPA found the practice to constitute misleading…
legal.summary: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has penalised Rapido ₹10 lakh for pre-ride tipping prompts that misled consumers. The regulator found that Rapido's design—prompting users to add tips before confirming their ride—created a false impression that additional payments would improve ride availability and booking confirmation speed. The CCPA classified the practice as a misleading advertisement under the Consumer Protection Act, an unfair trade practice, and a prohibited dark pattern. The order does not specify the date of the decision or name the presiding officer, but the finding hinges on the causal link Rapido established (intentionally or by design) between consumer payment and service quality improvement, which the regulator deemed deceptive. No appeal timeline or remedial orders (e.g., mandatory design changes) are mentioned in the excerpt.
legal.contextNote: This engages Section 2(47) (misleading advertisement) and Schedule II (dark patterns) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, enforced by CCPA under Section 60. The 'dark pattern' angle is material: India's DPDP Act (2023) does not yet operationalise equivalent UX-deception standards, but the CCPA's framing—design nudges that falsely correlate payment to service—may set precedent for fintech and ride-hailing compliance. (1) In-house teams at mobility and payment platforms should audit pre-transaction prompts, tip flows, and any UX element that could imply causation between voluntary add-ons and core service performance; the ₹10 lakh fine is a floor for established players. (2) Counsel should distinguish between optional tipping (permissible) and conditional framing (prohibited); Rapido's placement *before* ride confirmation, not after delivery, was the trigger. (3) Watch for CCPA guidance on fintech onboarding and digital wallet top-ups, which may face similar scrutiny if design implies speed-of-service correlation with incremental spend.
